title: Achu Soup (Yellow Soup) with Achu Coco
author: Imma Adamu (Immaculate Bites)
desc: Beef, tripe and cow skin simmered in stock, which is cooled, then blended with melted red palm oil, ground achu spice and ground limestone until it turns bright yellow and emulsified — poured over mashed steamed cocoyam.
longDesc: Adamu’s achu soup has two parts. The soup: assorted meats are boiled in stock with salt and red pepper about 30 to 60 minutes (a pressure cooker roughly halves it), the stock is cooled to room temperature and about 6 cups reserved, and the red palm oil is melted until liquid. The stock, oil, achu spice, ground limestone, salt and bouillon are blended until smooth and emulsified; the page says to look for a bright yellow colour. The achu coco is cocoyam steamed unpeeled until tender, peeled, pureed in a food processor or mortar, and salted. If the soup separates, the page says to add a little limestone and pulse again.
ingredients: 1–2 pounds (450–900 g) assorted meat (beef, tripe, cow skin, smoked fish, dried crawfish, etc.)
Salt, 1/2–3/4 teaspoon (3–4 g) per pound of meat
Ground red pepper to taste (or a whole Scotch bonnet)
6–7 cups (1 1/2 L) stock (or 6 cups water with 2 tablespoons beef bouillon)
1 tablespoon (10–11 g) bouillon powder or Maggi
equipment: Food processor or mortar and pestle
steps: Put the meat in a saucepan with salt, red pepper and the stock. Boil until tender, about 30–60 minutes or longer. A pressure cooker roughly halves it.
Remove the meat. Cool the stock to room temperature and reserve about 6 cups.
Heat the red palm oil until liquid (microwave or stove).
Blend the stock, warmed oil, achu spice, limestone, salt and bouillon until smooth and emulsified. The soup should turn bright yellow. Adjust the seasoning.
Steam the cocoyams (and green bananas, if using) unpeeled until tender. Rinse in cold water and peel.
Puree in a food processor or pound in a mortar. Salt it. Serve the meat with the yellow soup poured over, beside the achu.
chefTips: Printed cues: ‘bright yellow color’ and emulsified soup; cocoyam ‘until tender’.
If the soup separates, the author adds a little limestone and pulses again.
The steaming time for the cocoyam is not printed — test for tenderness.
commonMistakes: Blending hot stock with the oil instead of cooled stock.
Not checking the colour and emulsion before serving.
Over-handling the limestone: the page gives no safety guidance for it, so use a food-grade product.
storage: Leftovers keep 3–4 days refrigerated or 4–5 months frozen (page note).
healthBenefits: Meat adds protein; palm oil adds fat and colour; cocoyam is the starch.
culturalNote: Adamu writes that the dish is fairly common in the Western and North West provinces. Other pages tie achu to the Bafut or the Ngemba; those pages were weaker sources and are not used here. The page gives no safety guidance for limestone or for hot palm oil.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Achu Soup (Yellow Soup) & Achu’. Byline as printed: ‘Imma Adamu (Immaculate Bites)’. Published 7 Feb 2014, last update 30 Jan 2026. Yield 6. Prep 20 min, cook 1 h, total 1 h 20 min. Ingredients TWO-PASS; method SINGLE-PASS.
ABSENT, not estimated: cocoyam steaming time; limestone grade and any handling guidance; hot-oil handling.

Disagreements recorded: palm oil (1/2 cup here; 2 cups in CMR011; 190 g in CMR012), limestone (1 tablespoon here; ‘thumb size’ kanwa in CMR011; rock salt that is removed in CMR012), taro (4–5 pounds here; 2 kg in CMR012; 1 tuber plus 2 lb in CMR011).
